Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility: fact-checked peer-reviewed publication trusted source proofread The GIST Add to Preferred Sources Credit: illustrate Digital Ug from Pexels More than 2 billion people, or approximately one-quarter of the world's population, lack access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene, according to the United Nations Children's Fund . Today, 16 years after the U.N. General Assembly recognized this access as a fundamental human right , its legal protection is well established, but the reality on the ground lags behind. Protecting the human right to water means preventing harm before it occurs rather than assigning responsibility afterward, University of Notre Dame researchers argue in a new commentary published ahead of a major global water conference. Keough School of Global Affairs faculty members Ellis Adams and Diane Desierto—who also holds a joint appointment in the Notre Dame Law School—are among the authors of the commentary in Nature Water that calls for better implementation of universal water and sanitation access as part of the U.N.'s Sustainable Development Goals. They say a prevention-first approach can provide an effective blueprint to protect human rights for communities worldwide. The need to accelerate progress on safe water and sanitation will be on the agenda at the December 2026 United Nations Water Conference , co-hosted by Senegal and the United Arab Emirates. "We hope that this convening will help catalyze new ways for policymakers and practitioners to consider what more we can do as we approach the 2030 deadline for the Sustainable Development Goals," said Adams, associate professor of geography and environmental policy in the Keough School and a core-affiliated faculty member of the school's Pulte Institute for Global Development. Why prevention first In their commentary, the researchers called for focusing on how different actors, including private companies and government regulators, can help prevent harm from occurring in the first place rather than assigning responsibility once it has already occurred. Adams said one issue with looking backward is that harm sometimes surfaces long after the activity that caused it, making it harder to remediate. A mining company, for instance, might leave behind toxic chemicals from its work. Years later, when a community begins to show the effects, the company may be long gone or bought out by another company that hopes to avoid taking on damages. Desierto said that remediation may no longer be sufficient to restore the global water cycle to what it once was. "At this stage of our climate crisis, prevention is an inevitable strategy for an era of water inadequacy for present and future generations," said Desierto, professor of law and global affairs. "We need more proactive approaches in order to realize the human right to water and the related right to a safe, clean, healthy and sustainable environment." A contextual approach Adams said the approach links water-security and governance conditions to challenges in achieving clean water as a human right. Context is critical to protecting that right when communities have different views of what constitutes harm. "Water is never just water," said Adams, who is also affiliated with Notre Dame's Environmental Change Initiative and Eck Institute for Global Health. "When two communities say their right to water has been violated, it doesn't mean the same thing." Protecting the right to water requires understanding what water means to different communities. For one community, he said, the harm might be mining pollution that affects the food supply. For another, it may be water that's unsafe for mixing infant formula or making tea. For still others, it may be damage to a water site that is important for prayer, meditation or other cultural and religious activities. Laws and institutions matter too, he said. For example, in Chile, the 1981 water code long treated water as an economic good over a cultural one, so a mining company's use could take priority over a community's cultural claim. Subscribe Working with the private sector Companies in water-intensive industries—including mining, agriculture, beverage and garment—can integrate this approach into existing due-diligence processes that examine water risk, stewardship and human rights, Adams said. Such a move fits into the private sector's growing recognition of the need for corporate social responsibility, he added. That was the approach that Adams and other Notre Dame researchers presented to the U.N. at a 2022 forum in Geneva. They shared a framework aimed at helping communities realize water rights .
